Four Swedish top-flight campaigns have delivered 47 league goals. From Halmstad via West Yorkshire and Lancashire back to Scanian soil, the 32-year-old keeps finding ways to rattle the net.

Her kin issued a tear-streaked message, telling admirers on every continent of their sorrow. “We grieve to report that our mother, sister, grandmother, and great-grandmother died after a long fight against frontotemporal dementia. Her absence wounds everyone who held her close.”

Across fifty-three years Carr commanded boards and cameras alike. In 2017 doctors mapped shrinking tissue in her left temporal lobe. Shooting wrapped six months before she forgot how to switch the kettle on.

Producers, ushers, and teenagers who once waited at the stage door now flood social media with clips of her curtain-call smiles. The clan requests quiet space while they plan a small gathering in Central Park next spring; date and spot to follow once roses bloom.

Police officers and volunteers have combed every street, alley, and footpath within a three-mile radius of Keith’s home since sunrise on Monday. His daughter rang 999 at 18:42 on Sunday after the 71-year-old failed to return for his evening meal of fish pie and peas.

He stands 5 ft 8 in, weighs eleven stone, keeps his grey hair clipped to half an inch, and will not leave the house without his wire-rimmed spectacles. When he walked out he wore a cobalt polo shirt, indigo denim jeans, and polished black slip-ons. Relatives say he follows the river path to Riverside Park each dawn with a pair of worn binoculars to log sightings of kingfishers and herons.

By Tuesday the hashtag #FindKeith had appeared on 14,000 Twitter accounts, on the Facebook pages of birding groups from Cornwall to the Hebrides, and on the noticeboard of the Blackburn Roats supporters’ club. Sgt James Howard, who coordinates the search from a mobile unit parked beside the bandstand, repeated the plea: “If you spotted an older gentleman with binoculars after 17:00 on Sunday, call us at once.”

A single number, 0800 555 482, rings straight to a desk staffed round the clock by two detectives. Rachel Davies pressed start on a recorded message that plays to every caller: “Dad feeds the robins every morning; if he hears how frightened we are he’ll be crushed. Please look in your gardens, your sheds, your garages.”

Shopkeepers along Ormskirk Road have printed fresh posters on till-roll paper; pupils from three primary schools have formed human chains across recreation fields; a baker has promised free loaves to anyone who hands in dash-cam footage. Teams are now working through the reed beds where Keith once photographed a rare bittern.

Ring 0800 555 482 or dial 101 quoting log 1243 of 9 May if you know where Keith is. Officers also want doorbell videos captured between 16:30 and 19:30 on Sunday. The Davies family wait by the phone, counting the hours since he left.

A 33-year-old man stood before the court facing five charges after police stopped his silver Tamworth Proton Persona on Waterside’s main road at 23:15 on 12 April.

Traffic officers running a licence-plate camera check saw no record of current tax. When they waved the car over they found the windscreen disc slot empty, the insurance database blank, and no red L displayed front or rear. Moore, who holds only a provisional licence, sat alone behind the wheel; no supervisor aged twenty-one or older occupied the passenger seat. An officer smelled cider on his breath; a roadside breath test returned a borderline reading below the threshold for prosecution.

Moore was taken to Strand Road station, charged, and released on bail. His solicitor, John O’Donovan, told District Judge Joanna McHugh that his client had lost shift work in January and used the last £40 for rent rather than road cover. “He knows he was wrong and will pay whatever fine is set,” O’Donovan said.

Judge McHugh recorded the guilty pleas and adjourned sentencing to 9 May, warning that the maximum fine for each offence totals £5,000 and that she may endorse or revoke his licence. She advised Moore to book the driving theory test before the next hearing.

The court file will remain open until payment and proof of a valid policy are supplied.

Spain ruled the pitch in Alicante, moving the ball as if it were on rails. Ramos snapped into tackles, then stepped past the first press to spring counters, a white bandage blooming on his left thigh after a clash with Aspas. He waved the physio away and stayed on.

Iniesta surveyed the grass like a surveyor with a transit, threading balls between two blue shirts for Pedro to run onto. Each time the visitors thought they had him bracketed, he spun into the pocket they had just abandoned, leaving legs tangled.

Silva took more kicks than a training dummy, yet still flipped diagonal chips that dropped onto the penalty spot. One clipped the bar, another forced Casilla to claw wide.

Then Gaspar hurled himself skyward, connected with a dropping clearance, and smashed an overhead that tore the net before he landed. The stadium roared like a jet engine; del Bosque’s notebook flipped out of his hand.

In the closing stretch Isco shaved the post, Fabregas had a toe-poke smothered, but 1-0 held. The whistle sent 28,000 home fans into bounce-mode, scarves whirling above their heads.

Del Bosque found Gaspar first, thumping his back, then clasped Ramos by the neck, both grinning through sweat. The bus pulled out under a moonlit sky, headlights sweeping over fans who chanted “campeones” until the last taillight vanished.

Ministers now face the December 31 sunset of the seven-year brake that capped Romanian and Bulgarian hires when the two states entered the EU. Without that curb, every adult from those countries will gain an automatic right to take jobs on the same terms as French or Polish citizens.

Whitehall modelling predicts that 30 000 extra people could arrive within twelve months. If they sign on for job-seeker allowances, register with GPs, or join council-house lists, departments warn that budgets fixed in last October’s spending review will snap. To keep the books balanced, officials have drafted a three-year wait before new arrivals can claim housing benefit, child tax credit, or non-urgent NHS operations.

Critics in the Lords and charities such as Refugee Action call the plan discriminatory. They point to clauses that bar migrants from homeless hostels unless they have paid National Insurance for 104 weeks, and say GPs could refuse to accept new patients without proof of private insurance. Church leaders fear street homelessness will rise in Slough, Peterborough and Glasgow, where Romanian labourers already sleep in parked vans.

Home Office replies rest on a single line: “British taxpayers come first.” Theresa May told MPs on 3 June that councils in Birmingham and Kent had asked for emergency funds after Slovak and Latvian arrivals doubled waiting lists for nursery places. She will not retreat, though Lib Dem coalition partners threaten to abstain when the regulations reach the Commons before Christmas.

Behind the scenes, Downing Street has floated a softer option: keep the housing bar but allow GP registration after six months of work. Bulgarian diplomats counter that any second-class treatment breaches the EU treaties and will land the UK before the European Court before Easter. With only 192 days left until the gate lifts, civil servants are rehearsing two scripts: one for a climb-down, one for a court battle that could drag until 2017.

After marathon talks in Nyon, the board voted 17-3 to let domestic leagues pick their own kick-off windows, tearing up the 42-year-old centralised calendar that had fixed every Saturday at 15:00 and Sunday at 20:45 CET.

Detractors predict fixture pile-ups with Champions League nights bleeding into Monday prime-time slots. The EPFL counters that clubs can now stagger matches to avoid head-on clashes with NBA playoffs or Grand Slam finals, protecting gate receipts.

“This rewrites the calendar drawn in 1982,” the Swiss-based alliance said. “Every competition can map kick-offs to ticket-buying habits: Serie A might favour 18:00 for aperitivo crowds, while Scandinavia can book floodlit 19:00 slots before early-winter frost sets in.”

The same communiqué warns leagues not to treat squads like touring rock bands. Medical data from FIFA shows muscle strains spike when teams play three matches inside eight days; the EPFL will flag any club that logs more than 37 competitive hours in a 30-day stretch.

Ankle sensors and saliva cortisol kits will feed weekly dashboards shared with club doctors. If red-zone thresholds are crossed, panels of sports scientists can force a mid-season break.

Broadcast analysts at Mediapro forecast a 9–12 % uplift in domestic TV audiences once leagues align with local prime-time dramas rather than the old pan-European slot. Skeptics inside UEFA fear a Balkan league could dump a derby on the same evening as a Euro qualifier, leaving national coaches without key strikers.

The EPFL brushed aside such alarm, pointing to a built-in 48-hour buffer around FIFA windows. Leagues that ignore it risk losing solidarity payments worth €3.8 million per club.

“We trust chairmen who live beside their stadiums to know whether a snow-plough or a Ramadan fast shapes their crowd more than a Zurich clock,” the release closed.

Torquay United F.C., nicknamed the Gulls, ended months of rumors on Tuesday when Gaming International signed the final papers to buy the Devon club.

The Swindon-based betting-and-arcade firm, best known for racecourse slot halls and seaside leisure centres, now owns a football side for the first time. The price tag stays under wraps.

Clifford Baker, Gaming International’s chief, grinned through a Plainmoor press call:  
“We’re bringing the Gulls into the GI fold. A century-old badge, a drum-banging terrace, a coast that shuts down for away goals – that’s the brand of drama we want to back.”

He promised cash for a new training barn, a full-time data scout, and a ticket scheme that lets local kids in for a quid on Fridays.

Torquay’s last twenty years have yo-yoed between League One and the National League; last season they finished 17th in League Two. Gates slipped below 2,300 in February.

Supporters’ trust chair Donna Weekes posted a dawn selfie outside the ground: “New owner, new paint, new hope – let’s see where it goes.”

Joint staff meetings start Monday. The first visible change will be lime-green-trimmed shirts unveiled in July.

Whatever follows, fishermen on the harbourside will still belt out “Yellows, yellows” when the teams walk out on August 10.

Commissioners will convene at City Hall on Tuesday, 14 May, for the first joint public meeting in Welsh devolved history. Seats in the council chamber are free and open to anyone who arrives before 10:00 a.m.; overflow screens will operate in the foyer once the hall fills.

Children from Ysgol Hamadryad will sit beside pensioners from Roath. Farmers from Ceredigion will share the microphone with urban planners from Swansea. Each of the four commissioners—Future Generations, Children, Older People, and Welsh Language—will take questions for twenty minutes, then open the floor to a combined debate.

Questions already submitted include: How will the new curriculum guarantee fluent Welsh for every seven-year-old? What happens to coal-tip safety budgets if Westminster withholds £20 million? Can social-care staff be paid a living wage without raising council tax above 7%?

The session ends at 1:00 p.m. with a public commitment, signed by all four office-holders, to meet again in autumn and publish a shared action plan before Christmas.

UK citizens and residents can use the site to build and back petitions covering any topic Westminster could legislate on. Once 10,000 people have clicked “sign”, Downing Street must publish a written reply that spells out exactly where it stands. Hit 100,000 names and the petition qualifies for possible time on the Commons floor, pushing the issue under MPs’ noses.

The portal sits within the government’s open-data drive, built so a first-timer can launch a campaign in minutes: a plain-English form asks for the target, the demand and a short pitch, then serves advice on gathering supporters. Every live petition, signature count and ministerial reply sits in one searchable feed.

Rules keep the space workable: demands have to fall within Westminster’s remit, and moderators bin wording that crosses the line into abuse or libel.

A “Debates” page holds full Hansard logs of petition-triggered Commons sessions, letting backers watch the argument unfold bench by bench.

Altogether, the tool hands any voter a direct line to the green benches, turning a keyboard and postcode into a ticket to the legislative agenda.

Monza’s asphalt has swallowed more dreams than it has granted. Engines scream through the parkland at 205 mph while retaining walls wait like stone guardians; in 1978 a chain of collisions hurled cars into the grandstands and the race continued after the wreckage was dragged away. Only riders who treat braking markers as suggestions dare claim this place.

The loop stitches village alleys, royal park lanes and a 1.1-kilometre plunge toward the Parabolica. Curbs are knife-edged, run-off is cobblestone, and the only barrier between rider and lake water is a stripe of red paint. Elevation flips 26 metres in 300 metres, slamming ribs against tank on the way down and star-gazing the front wheel on the way up.

Seventeen corners demand gear-shifts timed to the hundredth-second; miss the first apex at Lesmo by a tyre-width and the exit speed bleeds 8 km/h for the next kilometre. Clouds rolling off the Alps can dump five millimetres of rain between lap 12 and lap 13, turning the racing line into a mirror while the outside stays dry.

A rider needs two gifts: the left hand must ease off brake pressure while the right cracks open throttle, and the brain has to re-write the track map every lap as rubber marbles swap places with drizzle. Picking the inside curb at Ascari can shave 0.14 s, but touch it two centimetres too early and the bike vaults into the trees.

Behind the pits a diesel generator thunders at 110 dB, powering laptops that model tyre-carcass temperature to the nearest 0.3 °C. A single mechanic can swap a seamless-shift gearbox in 92 seconds, fingers racing across dogs and selector forks while the rider watches the monitor, helmet still on.

Visor snaps shut; earplugs muffle the world to a dull roar. Alone inside carbon-fibre, the rider hears only intake howl at 14 000 rpm and the faint click of the quick-shifter. Tachometer needle blends with the wall’s coloured banners into one smear of light.

At 280 km/h the wind punches 160 kg against the chest, forcing lungs to work like bellows. Retinas can only lock onto the approaching kerb; everything else smears into peripheral streaks. Blinking costs 12 metres—three bike lengths—enough to overshoot the braking marker and meet the gravel at 4 g.

No red flag pauses the war inside the helmet. Pain is shoved aside until the forearm cramps into a claw on the final lap, yet throttle stays pinned because memory of last year’s defeat hurts more than lactic acid. The chequered flag waves once; if the timing beam catches the front tyre 0.001 s late, the story ends in silence instead of champagne.

Arrests jumped 38 % over last winter. ICE officers credit the rise to Donald Trump’s promise to swell the agency’s payroll and squeeze cities that bar police from handing jail inmates to federal agents.

Records filed in March show more than half of those picked up had never been charged with a crime. Non-criminal detentions climbed from 4 900 to 10 800 between January and March.

The weekly busloads of handcuffed riders rolling out of county lockups mirror the White House push to shrink the living space of anyone without papers. Agents have cuffed green-card holders fined for shoplifting two decades ago and cafeteria workers whose only file is a traffic ticket.

Even with the climb, ICE collars remain under the 2014 Obama-era high of 19 170. If agents keep the current pace they will top that record by December.

Church basements in Phoenix and Newark have turned into legal clinics overnight as parents draft standby guardianship letters. Lawyers call the raids “daylight kidnappings” that empty school pickup lines.

Supporters of the surge say the law is finally being read aloud. They note that Congress made every unauthorized presence a deportable offence long before Trump took office.

Critics reply that the spreadsheets reveal a wider dragnet, not a scalpel aimed at gang leaders. Nationwide, immigration court dockets have swollen by 200 000 new cases since February.

Cable panels, city-council chambers and PTA meetings keep spinning the same question: how many neighbours disappear before the economy built on their labour starts to wobble.

Leeds United cut the defender loose after twelve months when Bielsa’s rebuild left the 28-year-old on the fringe; only fifteen scoreless outings came from his year in West Yorkshire.  

A failed trial at Ibrox had pushed him toward Elland Road, yet the switch never caught fire.  

Now freed, he trains alone while St Johnstone, Aberdeen and Hibs circle; Tynecastle chatter cooled after Levein told radio reporters a reunion “isn’t on our radar.”  

His advisor insists the centre-half still bosses a box and will show it wherever pre-season begins.

The body will build a live certification system that every youth worker and workplace trainer must clear before they can practise. Live exams, shadowing shifts, and portfolio reviews will check whether staff can read a safeguarding cue, deliver a lesson at Grade 3 level, calm an anxious teen, and log the incident in the required two-hour window.

After the badge is issued, re-certification lands every twenty-four months. Each cycle mirrors new job duties, updated epilepsy protocols, and the shifting risks that surface in annual youth-voice surveys.

A 12-clause ethics charter will sit on the dashboard of every registered worker. The clauses name the exact lines that cannot be crossed: sharing a phone number, photographing a child, or leaking a case note. Breaches are logged in an open register that parents can search by postcode.

Anyone can lodge a complaint through an encrypted web form. A three-person panel—one lawyer, one clinician, one 18-year-old alumnus—reviews the file. Sanctions range from a £500 fine to lifetime removal from the register.

The body runs Friday twilight labs, Saturday micro-courses, and summer boot camps. Subjects rotate: suicide first-aid, VR careers demos, and how to write a risk assessment for a building site visit. Completion hours feed directly into re-certification points.

Random spot-checks will ride shotgun on every provider. Inspectors arrive unannounced, scan signed consent forms, and quiz the young people on what they were promised versus what they received. Centres that fail the spot-check lose their licence to operate within 28 days.

Adult diapers—worn every day by stroke survivors, nursing-home residents, mothers whose pelvic floors never fully healed—still copy the hourglass shape patented in 1948. Fader calls that frozen blueprint a warning that profit has outrun imagination.

At her Southampton lab she hacks the next layer of the problem: a sheet-thin textile that locks liquid into silica pockets, a waistband no thicker than a watch strap, and a printed circuit that pings a phone before skin stays wet for five minutes. Early prototypes cut night changes from three to zero in a trial of 112 residents.

The old plastic backing that rustled like a grocery bag has been swapped for a knitted bamboo panel dyed to match underwear tones; lab cameras show wearers forgetting they have it on. One volunteer, a retired teacher who once skipped her grandson’s wedding to avoid bulges under silk, now rides the bus to the seafront twice a week.

Fader’s next sprint pairs fibre optics with a cloud map of saturation patterns. Data from 4,000 nights will train an algorithm to predict leaks one hour ahead, giving carers time to adjust fluid schedules rather than react to soaked sheets. Grant money rides on proving that dignity can be measured in uninterrupted sleep hours.

Irish and North-Irish agencies now treat toxic debt like hazardous waste: isolate, shrink, and seal it.  
Dublin has opened an online ledger that tags every loan ninety days behind schedule; once tagged, the debt is auctioned to specialist buyers who collect or litigate. Belfast follows the same ledger but adds a clause that forces the buyer to keep the borrower in the property for at least six months.  

Regulators in both jurisdictions have raised the cash buffer a bank must hold against each new mortgage by two percentage points and now reject any application where repayments would top thirty-five per cent of net salary. Credit-unions must tape every loan interview and store the file for seven years.  

AIB and Ulster Bank have rolled out split-interest contracts: the first three years carry zero coupon while the principal is frozen; year four resets the rate to the ECB plus one per cent and stretches the term to age seventy. Permanent TSB grants a thirty per cent haircut if the customer surrenders a second car or buy-to-let flat within twelve months.  

Stormont’s finance unit meets HM Treasury every Friday to ring-fence EU-origin grants for small exporters so that sudden customs delays do not push viable firms into arrears.  

Dáil Éireann will publish a personal insolvency bill next month giving judges power to cap home-loan arrears at €250 000 and erase credit-card balances below €20 000 after five years of steady partial payment.  

Selling the face-value of a loan for twelve cents on the euro still leaves the borrower owing the full sum to a new master, and the watchdog admits the plan could push more households toward high-cost moneylenders. Officials will recalibrate the sale price floor every quarter using insolvency court data and suicide-prevention helpline logs.

Oldham’s 17th-place finish, only seven points clear of the drop, closed the curtain on his 14-month reign. Simon Corney, chairman since 2004, swallowed hard before pulling the trigger: “We owe him gratitude, yet the squad drifted. Staying up is no longer enough; we want a push toward the top half.”

A glittering playing résumé—three promotions and 47 caps—had not translated to the dugout. Supporters hammered his 3-5-2 switch at Carlisle and the benching of top-scorer Rowe; radio phone-ins blistered with calls for his head. He countered that the training-ground roof leaked, the transfer kitty held £30 k, and Tuesday-night trips to Plymouth left bruised calves and minds.

Driven home to Harrogate, he boxed up training bibs and corner-flag cones, then phoned his agent before the kettle boiled. “I still want to lead a dressing room,” he said. “Next time I’ll insist on clauses for pitch covers, data analysts, and a pre-season tour.”

Bookmakers link Oldham to John McGreal, Keith Curle, and a 35-year-old German who coached Hoffenheim’s under-19s. Whoever steps in on 1 July inherits a squad whose leading scorer netted nine and whose keeper tore a calf in April.

The July-to-September trading period gives clubs a second chance after May’s final whistle. Last season’s relegation fighters can swap the scrap for a sprint; champions-elect can bolt on the one piece they missed. One sharp deal in August can tilt the title odds before a ball is kicked.

Scouts spend June in South American airports and December evenings freezing in Nordic stands. They chase a 19-year-old winger whose release clause still has teenage acne, or a 29-year-old striker with 20 league goals and only twelve months left on paper. When the fax clears, finance directors sigh with relief as weekly salaries walk out the door alongside the surplus centre-half.

Lose your penalty-saving keeper on 1 July and by 3 July every set-piece drill feels like guesswork. The fax machine has to spit back a replacement or the back line learns to live without clean sheets.

Selling one home-grown midfielder to Manchester for £50 million keeps the training-ground lights on through January. A Ukrainian side sends two youngsters on loan with compulsory purchase clauses; the bank manager finally stops calling.

Supporters scroll phones at 11:58 p.m. on deadline day. If the only incoming name is an unknown Korean left-back, season-ticket renewals drop eight per cent. Announce a French World-Cup winner and the club shop sells 6,000 shirts before sunrise. Either mood lingers into April, when snow is still falling and the quarter-final draw is made.

The air vibrates with excitement as people drift onto the fairground under a Midwestern sky the color of a jay’s wing. White pickups and rented F-250s nose between the rows; interns in khakis sprint clipboards to folding tables, their breath puffing in early-morning vapor. Overhead, vinyl sheets snap in the breeze—each one silk-screened with a scowling eagle, talons locked around a lightning bolt—pushing the message that every success begins with one person alone.

Mitt Romney climbs the three-step riser to a thunder of applause. He has done this for twenty-five months straight; muscle memory steers him through the crowd. Left hand finds a shoulder, right hand squeezes a forearm, blue eyes lock on blue collars for the exact count of two heartbeats before he moves on. The suit is midnight wool, pressed so sharply it could stand by itself against the bleachers festooned in bunting.

Every sign within camera range repeats the same two-word demand: HIRE US. A state senator from Akron warmed the audience with a story about the stamping plant that closed at Christmas; the congresswoman from Toledo followed with a tale of a father who now drives 120 miles nightly for Amazon. By the time Romney grips the lectern, the word “jobs” has been spoken 47 times.

Outside the rope line, Ohio keeps its own ledger: 14,000 positions gone at the GM van plant in Moraine; 3,200 at the AK Steel blast furnace in Ashland; 900 at the copper-wire mill in Marion. Robots weld F-150s in Louisville instead of people; Chinese rolled steel lands at the Lorain docks for nickels on the dollar.

Behind the candidate, a three-story scaffolding supports a mural: four steelworkers in silver helmets guide a white-hot slab down a roller table. The image is a 1978 photograph from the now-shuttered Republic mill in Youngstown, blown up until each bead of sweat shows as a golf ball. Romney uses it as living evidence that America once bent iron and can again if Washington steps aside.

He ends with a vow to fuse California code to Ohio lathes—an app that matches displaced machinists to open shifts within fifty miles, tax credits for plants that retrain instead of relocate, visas for foreign engineers who agree to spend five years in Detroit rather than Palo Alto. The loudspeakers spit static on the final syllable, but the word already hangs in the air like the smell of cut grass and diesel: JOBS.

Fresh honors will spotlight the grind shown by footballers, trainers, and squads since last season.  
The extra trophies break down like this:

African Club of the Year: lands in the hands of the continent’s top side, the one that stacked trophies, clawed back from deficits, and kept climbing the rankings.  

African Coach of the Year: goes to the tactician whose game plans turned a mid-table unit into contenders or who shaped raw teenagers into match-winners.  

Most Promising Talent of the Year: tracks the 21-or-under star who left defenders on the turf and turned bench cameos into YouTube loops.  

Goal of the Year: singles out the strike no keeper reached—maybe a 30-metre dipper, a bicycle kick, or a solo slalom through four shirts.  

Fair Play Award: salutes the captain who owned up to a dive, the medic who sprinted to aid a rival, or the squad that clapped an injured opponent off the pitch.  

African Referee of the Year: handed to the whistle-blower whose red-card call survived VAR, whose added-time count was spot-on, and whose name never trended for the wrong reasons.  

African Women’s Player of the Year: crowns the striker who out-ran back lines, buried headers, and dragged her league gate past six figures.  

African Women’s National Team of the Year: goes to the side that parked the bus when needed, countered like lightning, and lifted a trophy or hit a historic ranking high.  

A jury of ex-captains, analysts, and scouts will lock the doors, replay clips, scan stats, and cast votes. The gala night in Marrakech will roll drums, drop spotlights, and hand out the golden figures.

Two cars split the night on the A470. Rhodri Miller’s black Golf carried Alesha O’Connor and Corey Price; Margaret Challis steered her green Polo a short distance behind. Both groups left the Storey Arms pass at speed. At 23:14 on 6 March 2015 their paths crossed an oncoming Peugeot. Metal folded, glass scattered, and all four died before the sirens arrived.

Barry’s Year 12 corridors emptied the next morning; St Richard Gwyn’s chapel bells rang for Alesha. Merthyr’s town square filled with flowers for Margaret. Parents pinned hoodies to railings; friends parked hatchbacks with headlights left on.

Merthyr council later parked a crumpled hatchback outside the college gate. Every learner driver now sits inside it before their first lesson, belted in while an instructor reads the crash report aloud. Road-side lessons replace classroom theory; speedometers are taped at thirty during initial drives.

Each June the four names are read beside the river bridge. A sponsored five-mile run raises cash for brake-light sensors supplied free to local sixth-formers.

Leinster must now plan without Johnny Sexton after scans confirmed a grade-three shoulder separation that will keep the 38-year-old out for at least five months, shredding the champions’ pre-season playbook overnight.

Television footage caught the instant when Connacht blindside flanker Seán O’Brien’s tackle drove Sexton’s right shoulder into the ground at the Galway Sportsground; the snap of ligaments was audible on the referee’s mic.

Cullen’s squad had arrived on the west coast chasing a double, yet left with neither trophy nor their general. Connacht’s rush defence hunted Sexton’s channel from the kick-off, and once he departed in the 11th minute the contest tilted irrevocably.

Surgeons reattached the torn acromioclavicular joint with two tight-rope screws; the arm will spend six weeks immobilised in a sling, ruling Sexton out of Ireland’s warm-up Tests and Leinster’s United Rugby Championship opener against the Sharks.

“Johnny is gutted, we’re gutted,” Cullen said in a brief club release. “The operation went as planned; now we wait.”

With the calendar already flipping toward July, Leinster’s brains trust must decide whether Ross Byrne’s 96 caps for the province provide enough authority, or whether 20-year-old Sam Prendergast’s left boot is ready six months early, or whether to chase a short-term deal for a World Cup-bound 10 cast adrift by another country.

They suspected shards of the downed plane lay locked in the dark Irish bog, a wet sponge of sphagnum and black water stretching between low hills. Old dispatch logs, a farmer’s memory of a 1943 fireball, and a drone-mounted magnetometer sent them walking the heather with backpacks and spades.

Villagers had been turning up scraps for seventy years: a rivet beside a drainage ditch, a buckle in a turf stack, a shard of plexiglass snagged on a sheep’s hoof. Each find carried a date and a grid reference; plotted together they drew a rough arrow across the moor.

They rented two rooms above the post office, laid plastic sheeting across the slate floor, and marked out fifty-metre squares. Day after day they sliced the top off the bog with long knives, fed the peat through a shaker table, and followed every squeal of the detector. Radar pulses painted ghost-images of aluminium ribs beneath three metres of moss.

Rain soaked their clothes; midges crawled inside collars; the bog exhaled a cold stink like rotting leather. Yet they kept cutting, because the war records ended with the word “unrecovered.”

Seven Tuesdays into the dig the blade struck metal: a two-metre section of skin still painted dull green, rivet lines intact. Trowels uncovered a starboard flap, then a Pratt & Whitney cylinder, then a scorched leather flying boot with the owner’s name inked inside. They lifted each piece on plywood sheets and wrapped them in acid-free tissue.

Conservators at the county museum freeze-dried the leather, rinsed the aluminium in citric acid, and hung the fuselage fragment where school groups now file past. Children ask why the metal smells of smoke; guides answer that the ground kept it honest.

The survey notes, the peat chemistry readings, and the magnetometer maps were copied into a field manual that other crews now follow when searching for buried aircraft in County Mayo and beyond. The method has already traced a Spitfire tail under a golf course and a Lancaster wheel in a compost yard.

Years later the same archaeologists still drive the same patched Land Rover, but the smell of wet peat can stop them mid-sentence, carrying them back to the morning they brushed soil from a name still readable on a boot tongue and learned the earth sometimes gives back what it hides.

The FA charged Chelsea midfielder Mikel Obi after he barged into Mark Clattenburg’s dressing room following the 28 October 3-2 loss to Manchester United at Stamford Bridge.

Official papers accuse Mikel of shouting threats and insults at the referee. If the panel rules against him he will be hit with a cash penalty and a ban. Fury gripped the Nigerian after team-mates told him Clattenburg had aimed a racial slur at him, a claim the Durham official flatly rejects.

Mikel has not contested the charge but asked to speak in person, the FA said. Chelsea back their player, insisting he reacted only after hearing the alleged abuse.

Detectives from the Metropolitan Police are running a parallel probe; the FA paused its own interviews so the two strands would not collide.

A guilty verdict usually brings a three- to eight-match ban plus a heavy fine.

Chelsea’s campaign already reads like a courtroom drama—boardroom exits, a sacked manager, now this. Mikel, signed in 2006 and capped 300 times for the club, would leave a hole in the midfield if sidelined. The final tally of games missed will be fixed once the last witness is heard.

Kinlochshiel kept crushing the schedule, milking every 1–0 or 2–1 for exactly one league point, nothing more. Week after week the streak grew: ten straight wins, then twelve, confidence climbing like the tally in the left-hand column.

Credit split two ways. First, the squad flipped shape mid-match, switching from a flat back four to a diamond when opponents overloaded wings. Second, coach Iain MacLeod read rival line-ups like sheet music, calling shifts that left rivals pressing shadows.

Centre-half Euan Campbell locked down six-goal strikers with tight shoulder pressure. In front of him, play-maker Lewis Smith dictated tempo, one-touch passes drawing markers out of lanes. Up top, striker Rory MacRae buried thirteen low drives inside the far post, keeping Kinlochshiel two points clear.

Pre-season friendlies had finished with leaky defeats to second-division sides; bookies tagged them 18-1 relegation candidates. Instead, they lost only once before the October break, then reeled off eight clean sheets in frost and sleet.

By December, travelling supporters wore black-and-yellow scarves knit by mothers and wives. Drumbeats echoed off the steel stand, smoke flares drifting over the touchline; players clapped back, sprinting to the corner flag after late winners.

Pressure peaked when league leaders Lochcarron visited with three rounds left. Kinlochshiel soaked up crosses, cleared one off the line in the 87th minute, then countered for a breakaway foul and a calmly rolled-in penalty that nudged them ahead for good.

Final-day odds still favoured Lochcarron on goal difference, but Kinlochshiel ground out a 1–0 dogfight on a rutted pitch, the winner bundled home after a keeper spill. They lifted the silver cup beneath floodlights while snow began to fall, the same team written off in August now engraved on the base as 2023 champions.

The paperwork landed on Tuesday: a four-year contract binding the 21-year-old to Sunderland AFC until 2027. David Moyes, who handed him his league debut in August 2022, had been calling twice a week since May, reminding him of the trust invested that night at the London Stadium.

Donald Love and Paddy McNair were already on Wearside, collected from Manchester United for £2.1 m and £2.9 m respectively. The three shared a dressing-room at Carrington in 2021, and the club’s analysts clocked 312 passes exchanged between them in one pre-season friendly; data that nuded the board toward a joint swoop.

Inside the Stadium of Light, season-ticket holders queued at the club shop to add the new surname to their shirts. The side had taken one point from the first twelve available; supporters hope the youngster’s diagonal switches and late third-man runs can tilt the midfield balance.

Moyes, speaking beside the pitch where the sprinklers hissed, recalled the first training session: “He clipped a forty-metre pass with the outside of his boot and hit the cone I’d placed on the penalty spot. I knew then I wanted him back.”

The transfer, financed by July’s outgoing broadcast rebate rather than fresh debt, pushes the wage bill back inside the league’s spending cap. Chairman Kyril Louis-Dreyfus told staff the manager’s job is secure through Christmas regardless of table position, citing promotion records at Everton and West Ham.

Love, McNair and the newcomer jogged out together for the open training session; children pressed against the barriers chanted a song set to the tune of ‘Seven Nation Army’. If the trio reproduce their old link-up, Sunderland’s last home win—April 2023—might finally have a sequel.

The order to shut down the Revolutionary Nationalist Youth (JNR) followed the fatal stabbing of a 19-year-old antifascist after a street fight in Paris’s 13th arrondissement on 5 June. The group, formed in 1987 by skinheads around Serge Ayoub, had already been linked to raids on punk concerts and attacks on migrants in Calais.

Counter-terror prosecutors in Paris have now opened a file tracing money and weapons between the JNR and the German group “Third Way”, the Italian “New Force” and the Greek “Combat 18”. Investigators traced a parcel of thirty extendable batons delivered from Dresden to Ayoub’s boxing gym in Montreuil last March.

Interior Minister Gérald Darmanin will present the decree outlawing the JNR at Wednesday’s cabinet meeting. If Emmanuel Macron signs, the 170 listed members must surrender passports, the gym will be sealed, and wearing the twin-lightning badge will carry a three-year prison term.

Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault told radio station RTL on Tuesday morning: “Republican law beats brass-knuckle law. We will strip them of their colours and their cash.”

Ayoub, 52, posted a grainy phone clip claiming “the reds staged their own ambush”. A separate clip, authenticated by police labs, shows him telling recruits on 12 April: “If they bring fists, bring boots; if they bring knives, bring bigger knives.” Doctors at Saint-Antoine hospital still treat Clément M., the student kicked into a coma during last year’s Book Fair brawl.

France has banned three far-right leagues since 2021; the JNR would be the fourth. Magistrates hope the legal template will next target the “Baroque Youth” and the “Hexagon Brigade”.

When Ashley Hoskin stepped aside in October 2015, the Chesterfield first-team coach took the reins. Drawing on five seasons of shaping League Two attacks at the Proact, he drilled the squad in the same 4-3-3 overload patterns that had lifted Chesterfield to 71 goals the previous year.

Inside six weeks, a ruptured ankle ligament to the starting left-back and back-to-back fixtures against the league’s top two could have sunk the side. Instead, he switched to a back five, promoted the U-21 skipper, and took four points from those games. Between training-ground video clips and 5 a.m. scouting runs to the Midlands, he added a Danish winger on a free and turned the reserve striker into a pressing machine.

Every setback drew the same grin and a whiteboard. Dressing-room decibel readings—tracked on the analyst’s iPad—jumped from 68 dB to 91 dB after wins. By March, the club had climbed eight places, posting its best goal difference since 1998.

Senior pros still talk about the Tuesday “two-touch trial,” a finishing drill where he kept score on a chalk wall. One player said the public ranking “made you chase extra reps.” Another credited the GPS-triggered sprint clocks for shaving 0.3 seconds off his 10-metre time.

He refused to let the squad accept “decent.” After a 3–0 derby humiliation, he replayed every lost duel on the big screen, then ordered a double session of shoulder-to-shoulder tackles on the narrowest training pitch. They won the return fixture 2–0.

Season after season, league positions rose: 14th, 9th, 5th, then automatic promotion sealed with a last-minute header on the final day. Staff who once called him “the rookie” now greet him by his nickname etched on the tunnel wall—proof that the lessons learned beside the Spireites have taken root for good.

Gillian met Rachel and Nyomi in the back room of Left Bank Books, where the club discussed "The Blind Assassin" over espresso pulled by the owner. All three women owned hairless sphynxes named after Victorian poets—Gillian’s cat answered only to Algernon. Talk slid from Atwood to latte foam art to the cats’ preference for warmed blankets, and by closing they had exchanged keys and sworn a blood-oath with paper-cut fingers.

When Rachel’s water broke at 3:07 a.m., Gillian arrived with a Coleman cooler packed with plunger coffee and a playlist of lullabies arranged for ukulele. For the next eighteen months she logged 2,847 night-time visits: she rocked Liam during bouts of colic, stitched cartoon patches onto cloth nappies, and once drove to Wilmington at dawn to fetch hypoallergenic formula. The child’s first laugh sounded like a bicycle bell; Gillian recorded it on her phone and set the clip as her morning alarm.

The invitations stopped without ceremony. Gillian’s calls rolled to voicemail. When she dropped by with board books and oat-milk lattes, Rachel opened the door six inches, blocking the hallway with her hip. Behind her, Nyomi scooped Liam up so fast his head snapped back. Gillian blamed herself until the neighbor, Mrs. Alvarez, whispered that the couple had been repeating lies about her at Pilates class.

The truth arrived on a Tuesday: Liam showed up at story-time covered in yellowing bruises shaped like thumbprints. Gillian blocked the exit and lifted his shirt—his ribs carried the same five-finger pattern. Rachel’s voice went flat: “Mind your own business.” Nyomi hissed, “You’re not family.” Gillian staggered out, vomited beside the book-drop, and dialed 911 from the parking lot.

Detective Ramirez took the report but needed forty-eight hours for a warrant; by Friday the Fees’ lease had been shredded, their phones disconnected, their Subaru gone. A postcard postmarked Phoenix arrived six weeks later—no return address, no signature—bearing a single line: “He’s ours.” Liam died in a motel bathtub two months after that; the coroner listed the cause as “blunt-force trauma to the abdomen.”

Gillian sold her condo, moved into a studio above the animal shelter, and now speaks at middle-school assemblies, handing out wallet cards that list hotline digits in bold ink. She keeps Algernon on a heated cushion by the door, the cat’s ears twitching each time the phone rings, as if the bell might be Liam’s laugh returning.

Ray, Tony, Mackey and Eddie spent three weeks driving Kirkcaldy’s grid of council streets, hunting a lone target. Word said Dwayne Kinner, small-time dealer, kept a week’s takings in his flat.

They picked the coldest Tuesday of January. For two nights they watched from a rust-coloured Vauxhall, timing who left and who stayed. Only Dwayne and cousin Nicholas remained after midnight.

They forced the Yale lock at 01:14. Tony and Mackey slipped toward the kitchen; Ray and Eddie climbed the narrow stairs. The pair were on the bed, controllers clicking, FIFA commentary crackling. Outside, dogs stopped barking.

Eddie nudged the door wide. “Talk, Dwayne. Where’s the gear?”

Dwayne paused the game, set the pad on the duvet. “Who says I’ll chat?”

Downstairs, drawers clattered, cupboards thuded. Nothing. The tip-off had lied; no brick of cash, no plastic-wrapped cocaine. Tony’s voice carried up: “Empty.”

They herded the cousins into the front room. Two pistols levelled.

Dwayne laughed, loud in the small space. “Thought you’d waltz out with my rent money?”

Eddie shoved steel against skin. “Try me.”

Nicholas sprang first. He shoulder-barged Mackey, snatched the machete from the coat stand, blade flashing. Dwayne twisted free, sprinted for the rear exit.

Robbery flipped to brawl. The four intruders back-pedalled through the hall, bleeding, stumbling over boots. Their score had vanished; the hunters now prayed to reach the street alive.

Inside Notre Dame, stone ribs caught the low murmur of 2,800 Parisians who had squeezed into the nave. No one spoke while the bourdon bell—nine tonnes of bronze—swung twelve times for the 130 dead. Each slow clang shook dust from the galleries and settled on black coats like grey snow.

François Hollande stepped to the lectern, collar tight, eyes ringed red. “We hurt,” he said, voice cracking against the vault, “but we close ranks the way these walls close around us.” He paused, let the echo die, then added: “They want us splintered; we answer by standing in the same breath.”

In row fourteen, Karim held the hand of the nurse who had stitched his left arm after the Bataclan. Both still flinched at sudden clicks—sounds like magazines sliding home—yet they rose when the organ sounded, backs straight as bayonets. Across the aisle, Claire clutched a photo of her daughter Lola, killed on the terrace of La Belle Équipe. Tears slipped off her chin and dotted the frame glass, but she did not wipe them away; she let them pool until the picture blurred into candlelight.

When the last bell faded, the doors opened onto the parvis. Outside, the Seine carried the city’s lights in wrinkled gold strips. No sirens, no horns, only footsteps and the soft click of Claire’s heels as she walked north toward the 11th, photo still in hand, drying in the night wind.

Lucas limped home last in his debut, engine coughing, tires shredded. He spent the next two weeks in the garage, stripping the wrecked chassis to bare metal, re-welding every cracked joint with fresh beads that glowed orange under the arc-flash. When the grid lights blinked green at Monza, he launched off the line hard enough to leave rubber ghosts on the asphalt and took the checkered flag by half a car-length.

From Spa to Suzuka the calendar threw new nightmares: monsoon cloudbursts, brake-fade at 320 kph, a Sauber that kept drafting then diving inside at the hairpin. Lucas answered with bleeding knuckles on the wheel, left boot bruised from pounding the clutch, visor fogged with sweat that tasted of iron. He ran the curbs so often his vertebrae rattled like loose bolts, yet he kept the throttle pinned, trusting the down-force to suck him back onto the racing line.

Sleep became a rumor. He lay in the motor-home listening to rain drum the roof, replaying apex speeds until the alarm chirped 4:45 a.m. Mechanics found him already in nomex, spooning cold oatmeal, eyes red but steady. Between races he sat alone in the paddock, forearms submerged in a cooler of ice, watching other drivers joke with sponsors; he stayed until the water lost its chill, then signed every autograph pressed against the fence.

Seven podiums out of nine rose like monuments carved from exhaust smoke: silver in Monaco after a last-lap dive, gold at Silverstone when he passed two cars through Maggotts-Becketts side-by-side, bronze at Interlagos under floodlights while the crowd chanted his surname. He lifted each trophy overhead, felt the heft of metal still warm from the printer, and thought only of the gearbox that had seized in race one.

The headlines flipped: from “Lucas Out of His Depth” to “Seven-Time Winner Seals Title.” Television crews wanted the glory sound-bite; he handed them a grease-stained notebook instead, pages filled with lap-time deltas and camber settings. Asked what changed, he shrugged, said he’d learned to weld faster than he broke.

The council shifted its gaze to other ledgers after townspeople packed the hall to defend the bookmobile, the Sunday concert series, and the tiny branch library on Oak Street. By voice vote they rejected the plan to erase those line-items; the proposed cut died on the floor.

A second motion—to raise meter fees from one dollar to two—stalled when shopkeepers produced receipts showing Saturday sales already down thirty percent. Petitions signed by 1,247 residents reinforced the message, so the idea was shelved for the year.

Finance staff now hunt for cash in three places: an emergency grant from the state capital, LED retrofits for the 1927 City Hall that trim the light bill by eighteen thousand a year, and tighter purchase-order rules that stop departments from buying new chairs without a surplus voucher.

Buyers are re-bidding the snow-plow salt contract, the IT help-desk agreement, and the janitorial schedule at the recreation center. Tax notices that went unopened last spring are being mailed again with a 2 % late fee. A bakery on Main has offered to host a weekend street market; the city will waive permit fees and take ten percent of stall rentals.

Council chair Vera Lopez closed the night by saying, “We will close the gap without taking books from kids or customers from storefronts.” The chamber applauded, then quieted: a 2.3 million dollar shortfall still waits in the next fiscal column.

The push for Scotland to leave the UK began long before 2014, yet support has surged since then. The SNP framed the 2014 ballot as the party’s flagship goal; 45 % backed leaving, 55 % chose to stay. “Scotland must go its own way” still echoes in town-hall meetings, printed on leaflets that cite North Sea revenue, EU membership, and centuries-old legal codes.

Westminster holds 591 seats that Scotland cannot touch. When every Scottish council voted to stay in Europe, English and Welsh ballots dragged the nation out regardless. That memory fuels claims that Holyrood is out-voted on trade, migration, and farming subsidies.

Brent crude still pumps east of Aberdeen; fields like Clair, Buzzard, and Mariner hold an estimated 1.5 billion recoverable barrels. Add onshore wind farms already powering two million homes, langoustine landings worth £180 million a year, and whisky exports topping £4 billion, and campaigners picture a treasury no longer sent to London.

Scots law requires corroboration, gives third-year students the “diploma in legal practice,” and still allows a “not proven” verdict. Gaelic road signs greet drivers on the A82, while the kirk’s parish structure predates Henry VIII’s break with Rome. Advocates say these traits fade when folded into a unitary British narrative.

Yet secession brings hazards: Would pensions keep paying in sterling, the euro, or a new currency? How long would border checks on the A1 last? Would Spain wield a veto over fresh EU accession talks to deter Catalonia?

The quarrel splits villages, workplaces, and families. Some demand another vote before 2026; others insist the 2014 tally should stand for a generation.

Brian stepped into the presidency brandishing open contempt for the rot that had spread through every ministry and backroom deal. He had sold voters on glass-wall governance, yet the real war started after the oath. Swearing to haul back the fortunes siphoned off by earlier regimes, he set out to revive the trust of citizens ground down by decades of empty excuses.

Breakfast on his first morning in office came with a single signature: a decree that birthed a graft-hunting body outside the grip of any cabinet member. Its brief was to map how cash vanished under five preceding governments. The roster read like a midnight raid on elite talent—an ex-Interpol money-laundering specialist who once flipped a cartel accountant, a Swiss-trained auditor who had traced a dictator’s gold to a Geneva vault, and a homicide detective who kept a wall of thank-you letters from widows.

The depth of the looting stunned even Brian. Lobby firms registered on the same street as the presidential palace had written every clause of the tax code for twenty years; four conglomerates held more sovereign debt than the central bank. Each file the commission pried open spat out another thicket of shell firms, and each revelation drew a louder chorus calling for his removal.

Night after night, Brian hunched over coffee-stained spreadsheets, linking wire transfers from a state airline upgrade to a London pied-à-terre bought for a retired general’s poodle. The paper trail snaked through Cayman trusts, a Ljubljana beer company, and a yacht registry in St. Vincent before circling back to buy a judge a private island.

By the fourteenth month, handcuffs clicked on a former vice-president at dawn on a Tarmac; soldiers dragged a shipping magnate off a chartered 747; and a court froze 117 city-center blocks bought with diverted disaster-relief funds. The arrests cracked a culture of immunity that had stood since the last century.

Reprisals followed like monsoon rain. A parcel of explosives arrived addressed to Brian’s wife; snipers fired on the commission’s convoy outside Mendoza; and a senate panel drafted articles of impeachment before sunrise. Brian kept the scheduled town-hall in a basketball gym that evening, walking in without a bulletproof vest.

When his six-year term expired, investigators had wired 2.3 billion dollars back into the treasury’s ledger—short of the haul he had once imagined, enough to build two subway lines and vaccinate every child born the next decade. He handed the sash to his successor beneath a cloud of confetti mixed with tear gas, the job unfinished yet the standard raised.

Robin Bevan, head teacher at a Southend school, recently condemned the practice of pinning digits to slices of pupil behaviour and achievement, warning that the habit breeds confusion and misreading.

At the last governors’ session he said that tidy scores shrink sprawling classroom realities into a single cell on a spreadsheet, lulling adults into trusting the “data” and quietly eroding real teaching. What slips away, he said, is the stuff that cannot be touched: a shy child’s first question in class, the steady gain in confidence after a parents’ divorce, the moment a poem finally makes sense. These events refuse to sit inside a 7, 4 or 91.

Figures cannot hold the shifting pace of any learner’s year, Bevan told the room. “School is not a measuring tape,” he said. “It is a living mix of personal growth, home life and the daily weather of feelings.”

Digits parade as exact, he warned, yet they push families and staff to act on mirages. A pupil who owns a 90 in science can still be clock-watching through lessons pitched too low; the grade hides the stall.

“Each child brings a private story—what sparks curiosity, what keeps them awake at night, what slang they speak with friends,” Bevan said. “A lone digit erases that story.”

He sketched other ways to chart progress: staff meeting to swap notes on reading habits, ten-minute pupil interviews each fortnight, wall-space for projects that refuse rubric boxes—robotics prototypes, spoken-word films, charity plans.

Such moves demand a new public picture of school, he added. “We need to stop sorting children like racehorses and start studying what each one could become.”

Bevan’s stand adds weight to the growing staff-room unease over league tables. Any overhaul will need slow conversation in halls, offices and kitchens before digits lose their grip.

Blair Turgott fought the full ninety like a man tugging a crate uphill by his teeth. Each blade of grass at Grange Lane seemed to snap at his ankles; opponents chopped at his calves, yet he kept showing for the ball, socks sagging, shirt tugged out, eyes still fixed on the far post.

With seven minutes left the stands smelled of nerves—hot coffee, colder doubt—until Turgott hunted a loose clearance on the left touchline. He nudged it infield to the rookie midfielder, sprinted past two shirts, demanded it back, then clipped a first-time diagonal that split the retreating back line. The pass rolled like a marble along a groove and stopped dead on the penalty spot.

Turgott kept running. The winger’s cross hit him at knee-height. He levered the ball upward with the inside of his boot, arcing it over the lunging keeper. The net billowed. 1-0.

A hush, then a roar that rattled the floodlights. Supporters poured from the terraces; stewards gave up the chase. Turgott stood near the corner flag, arms out, letting the noise crash over him while the referee glanced at his watch and whistled.

Grange Lane’s lights flickered on, spilling amber over a pitch now carpeted with celebrating strangers. Someone handed Turgott a scarf; he swung it above his head, laughing, breath clouding in the cooling dusk.

Terry, who joined Chelsea at fourteen, will leave when his deal expires, closing a twenty-two-year Stamford Bridge chapter. The centre-back, who collected five league winner’s medals, five FA Cups, three League Cups, a Champions League and a Europa League in 717 games, told followers on Instagram:

“Pulling on the blue shirt has been the honour of my life. To lead the team and share a dressing room with top-class footballers gave me days I will replay forever.”

A hamstring tear and ankle damage restricted him to nine starts this season. Once his medical team ruled him out of the run-in, the club and player agreed there would be no 12-month extension.

Bookmakers make him 2-1 to take a first manager’s post next term, 5-1 to sign for an MLS club, and 8-1 to appear as a television analyst.

He signed off: “Thank you to every supporter who sang my name. Your banners, letters and voices pushed me on. I will keep them with me wherever I go.”

Chelsea have yet to confirm whether they will stage a farewell fixture in his honour.

Clare Shine slammed three balls past the keeper in 73 electric minutes, every strike different.  
First, she ghosted past two defenders on the left channel, rolled her studs over the ball to freeze a third, then whipped a low drive inside the far post.  
Ten minutes later the keeper spilled a routine cross; Shine pounced, prodding the loose ball through a forest of legs from eight yards.  
Her third arrived on the break: a one-touch release from midfield sent her sprinting clear, she veered right, chopped back left, and arced a rising shot that clipped the underside of the bar.

Those finishes turned a tight quarter-final into a 5-1 rout and stretched the club’s winning run to 19 matches dating back to March.  
Shine now tops the season chart with 11 goals in 9 games; coach Luis Cantó says she clocks an extra 20 minutes of finishing practice after every session, chasing top-corner targets clipped to the frame of an empty net.

Online booking portals have redrawn the map for reserving vacations, weekend escapes, business hops, and everything between. A single screen links seats on planes, beds in hotels, keys to cars, and tickets to zip-lines or museums.

One 2022 survey by Phocuswright clocked the average session on these sites at four minutes from search to payment, compared with forty-three minutes spent calling airlines and hotels separately. Servers never close; a traveler on night-shift in Manila can lock in a dawn departure from Lisbon while the corner travel office sleeps.

Aggregators pull live inventory from 400-plus carriers, 2.8 million properties, and 180 rental brands onto one dashboard. Filters for departure time, baggage allowance, room square-footage, or hybrid-engine size let shoppers line up rivals side-by-side instead of hopping between thirty browser tabs.

Hoteliers and carriers gain billboard space they could never afford alone. Arthur Cory, first-born to the late Lord Penllyn, now holds the keys to Penllyn Castle, a limestone fortress outside Cowbridge where his bloodline has lived since the 1300s. In a pantry under the north tower he noticed a cedar-lined cupboard whose latch had not been oiled in decades. Inside lay a rolled banner stiff with salt-stiffened linen; candle-wax drips, sword nicks, and mended tears mapped every journey it had ridden.

The dragon on the cloth—vermilion on white-over-green—once flew from the stern of Lord Penllyn’s converted trawler when he patrolled Cardigan Bay during the war. Later it draped the mantelpiece in his rooms at Jesus College, Oxford, where he read history and sang in Welsh until dawn. Marriage, estate taxes, and a seat in the Lords pushed the banner into darkness; the cupboard door shut in 1973.

After the funeral Arthur lifted the roll, wiped off grey dust, and felt the snap of linen as it opened like a sail catching wind. Colours held: coch still bright as rowan berries, gwyrdd sharp as grass after rain. He spread it across the oak table where estate books lay open for lambing tallies. Aunt Mabel, ninety-four and living in the gatehouse, told him the flag had wrapped his father the night he was born during the blizzard of 1921. She remembered Lord Penllyn marching through Aberystwyth with the banner hoisted on a broomstick after Wales beat England at rugby in 1953.

Arthur traced a burn hole near the hoist; Mabel said a spark from a bonfire on the castle lawn had caused it the night they sang “Myfanwy” until the moon set. He telephoned three of his father’s crewmates from the coastal patrol; each recalled the same detail: when the sonar pinged a U-boat, Lord Penllyn tied the flag to the jackstaff so the dragon faced seaward. They laughed at the memory of German shells punching the water while the dragon kept flying.

That evening Arthur carried the banner upstairs to the nursery where his twins slept. He folded it small enough to fit the old pine chest that once held lead soldiers. When the boys wake, he will show them the dragon and teach them the chorus their grandfather belted out after every try.

Brent crude climbing above 85 dollars a barrel has lifted wholesale petrol, diesel and jet kerosene by matching margins. Sir Nicholas Winton, a London stockbroker, scrapped his Swiss ski trip in December 1938 after a phone call from Prague. He boarded the next train to Czechoslovakia carrying only a suitcase and a list of names supplied by Doreen Warriner’s refugee committee.

Prague’s railway station teemed with parents clutching toddlers and worn envelopes stamped with exit permits. Nazi troops had swallowed the Sudetenland three months earlier; now the capital waited for the rest of the country to vanish. Parents pressed photographs into Winton’s pockets, whispering train schedules and British addresses they had never seen.

Inside a rented room above Wenceslas Square, Winton spread city maps across the floor. He matched each child to a departure date, a berth on the Harwich ferry, and a foster home scraped from synagogue noticeboards and Rotary Club newsletters. By day he queued at the British consulate for £50 guarantor bonds; by night he typed transit cards on a borrowed typewriter whose ‘e’ key kept sticking.

On 14 March 1939, the first group—twenty boys in wool caps, one girl clutching a porcelain dog—left Wilson Station at dawn. Winton knelt to tighten their shoelaces, then stayed on the platform until the locomotive smoke thinned. Nine more trains followed before Hitler closed the borders on 1 September. The final departure carried 251 children and one suitcase labeled “Handle kindly—toys inside.”

In London, Winton stored forged travel permits beneath tins of flour in his Maida Vale flat. He bribed a Dover customs officer with Players cigarettes, then convinced Home Office clerk Beatrice Wellington to stamp visas after hours. When bombs shattered Liverpool Street Station in 1940, he rerouted evacuee trains through Cambridge and wired foster families from a post-office kiosk: “Child arriving 3 p.m. Name sewn in coat.”

After the war he sold typewriter ribbons, coached Sunday football, and never mentioned Prague. In 1988 Grete Winton handed her husband a dusty scrapbook while clearing the attic; inside were 802 photographs, a page for each child, plus a pressed snowdrop from the platform. That evening BBC’s *That’s Life* host Esther Rantzen showed the album on live television. A woman in the studio audience stood up, pointed to a picture, and said, “That’s me, 1939. Thank you, Nicky.”
